analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to let workers earn up to seven paid sick days a year.
analysis.headline: Referred to three House committees the day it was introduced, the bill never received a markup, vote, or floor action, and it died with the 116th Congress despite 161 cosponsors, including 160 of 231 House Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require employers with 15 or more workers to let employees earn one hour of paid sick leave for every 30 hours worked, capped at 56 hours — about seven days — per year. Workers could use the time for their own illness or medical care, to care for a child, parent, spouse, or partner, or to deal with domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking. Employers with fewer than 15 workers could opt out of paid leave but would have to provide 56 hours of unpaid leave, and the Labor Department and workers themselves could enforce the rules in court.
analysis.who_benefits: The tens of millions of workers without paid sick time. The bill's findings note that 29 percent of private-sector workers had no paid sick time, rising to 55 percent among the lowest-paid quartile, and more than 80 percent of food preparation and serving workers. Those workers would gain the ability to see a doctor, recover from illness, or care for a sick child without losing pay or their job, and victims of domestic violence would get protected time to seek safety, medical care, or legal help.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers without paid sick leave, especially low-wage workers

how_it_helps.text: Employers with 15 or more employees must provide at least 1 hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours a year, usable for the worker's own illness or medical care, to care for a child, parent, spouse, domestic partner, or close relative, or for needs arising from domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking.

The bill makes it unlawful for employers to interfere with or retaliate against workers who use sick time or file complaints, and it lets the Labor Department investigate violations while employees can sue in federal or state court for lost wages and reinstatement.

Paid sick time carries over year to year, accrues from the first day of work, is reinstated if a worker is rehired within 12 months, and state or local laws with stronger protections are not preempted.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 15 or more employees bear the wage cost of up to 56 hours of paid leave per worker per year plus the administrative work of tracking accrual, posting notices, and handling doctor's certifications for absences longer than three days. Businesses with fewer than 15 employees escape the paid requirement if they opt out, providing only unpaid leave instead.

drawbacks.text: The mandate shifts the cost of up to 56 paid hours per worker per year onto employers, and businesses facing that cost could respond by holding down wages, raising prices, or limiting other benefits; the bill does not reimburse employers.

Employers must keep compliance records, post notices, and may require doctor's certification for any absence longer than three consecutive workdays, adding administrative work, and workers without health insurance face uncertainty about how to provide certification.

Employers with fewer than 15 employees may opt out of paid sick time entirely and provide only 56 hours of unpaid leave, leaving workers at the smallest businesses with protection that costs them income to use.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is large and targeted at the workers least likely to have it: roughly three in ten private-sector workers, and over half of the lowest-paid quartile, had no paid sick time. The cost is real but capped — a maximum of seven days per employee per year, no payout at separation, and a small-employer opt-out — so the tradeoff is favorable to workers, with the burden falling on employers of low-wage workforces such as food service and retail. The main honest criticism is that paid time off does not help workers whose illness lasts beyond 56 hours, and that the smallest employers' unpaid-leave option offers little practical relief.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to three committees the day it was introduced; none of them ever took it up, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: DeLauro introduced the bill on March 14, 2019, and it was referred the same day to the Committees on Education and Labor, House Administration, and Oversight and Reform, with further assignment left to the Speaker.
The full action history shows no further action of any kind — no markup, no committee vote, no floor consideration — before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
The bill drew 161 cosponsors: 160 of 231 House Democrats and 1 of 197 House Republicans, meaning a majority of the full House had gone on record in support before it stalled in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have owed the new paid sick leave, especially in low-wage service industries, avoided the cost; the roughly three in ten private-sector workers without paid sick time continued to work without it, including through the early months of the pandemic.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who would have paid the leave

sides.party_line_note: 160 of 231 House Democrats and 1 of 197 House Republicans cosponsored the bill, and no vote was ever taken in committee or on the floor.

industries.industry: Employers of low-wage service workers (food service, retail, hospitality)
industries.note: These industries would owe the new paid leave and would absorb the largest new labor cost, since their workforces are the ones with the least existing paid sick time — more than 80 percent of food preparation and serving workers lacked access. Their interest in blocking or avoiding the mandate runs directly against the workers the bill would cover.

industries.industry: Small employers with fewer than 15 employees
industries.note: They could opt out of paid sick time and provide only 56 hours of unpaid leave, keeping their costs low while still adding recordkeeping and notice duties. Their workers, however, get protection they have to forgo pay to use.

The bill's findings cite evidence that paid sick time leads workers to seek earlier and routine care instead of deferring it or using emergency rooms, meaning more use of doctor visits and preventive care. That use aligns with the public health rationale for the bill.
